home.heroTitle: Real HTML. Zero JavaScript you didn't ask for.
home.heroSubtitle: Nexa compiles every page to real HTML — with SEO, i18n and real data — and only ships JavaScript to the nodes that actually need it. No empty bundle just in case.
home.codeCaption: A real Nexa page. This is all it takes:
home.adv1Body: A page with no interaction compiles to plain HTML. No runtime, no hydration, no empty bundle just in case.
home.adv2Body: Every interactive node declares its own strategy: interaction, visible, idle, load, or manual.
home.adv3Body: Valid title, meta tags, Open Graph and JSON-LD, generated per page — with an analyzer that warns when something's missing.
home.adv4Body: A dashboard or a complex cart mounts with your favorite framework, without the rest of the site stopping being HTML-first.
home.adv5Body: Every generated file carries a hash of its own content — a redeploy never serves stale JS or CSS from a visitor's cache.
home.adv6Body: The same project ships a real desktop binary (Tauri) or a real APK (Capacitor), without rewriting anything.
home.adv7Body: connectSSE/connectSocket wrap native EventSource/WebSocket in reactive signals — notifications, chat, live dashboards.
home.adv8Body: load() makes a real HTTP GET against any backend you already have — PHP, Go, Node, whatever. Nexa doesn't impose its own.
home.platformsTitle: Web, desktop, Android and iOS — without rewriting anything
home.platformsSubtitle: The same source code that compiles to real HTML for the web also packages into a real desktop binary or a real mobile app. No separate web build and native build to maintain.
home.platformWebBody: Chrome, Firefox, Safari — the same real HTML as always, indexable and with nothing to install.
home.platformDesktopBody: Windows, macOS and Linux with Tauri — a real, runnable desktop binary, built with cargo.
home.platformDesktopCode:
nexa add tauri
cd src-tauri && cargo build
home.platformAndroidBody: A real APK built with Gradle via Capacitor — verified end to end with a real Android SDK.
home.platformAndroidCode:
nexa add capacitor
npx @capacitor/cli add android
cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebug
home.platformIosBody: Same Capacitor mechanism as Android — generates a real Xcode project. Needs macOS to build; not verified in this Linux environment.
home.storyBody: The lotus at the center is purity and rebirth, the same symbol from Nezha's (哪吒) myth. Around it, a single wheel of fire evokes his wind-fire wheels and divine momentum. Jade, gold and red connect the mythical with the modern.
home.stat2Label: JS on a page with no interaction
home.stat3Label: languages, using the framework's own i18n
home.stat4Label: real HTML, indexable without running JS

compat.title: Compatibility
compat.intro: Nexa is backend-agnostic and cross-platform on the client. Here's what's verified today, and what isn't yet.
compat.backendsBody: Any HTTP backend that answers JSON: load() makes a real GET against the URL you declare. Verified against a real PHP backend in Nexa's own reference project; it works the same with Go, Node, Python, Java, or whatever you already have — the contract is HTTP + JSON, not a proprietary SDK.
compat.browsersBody: Any modern browser with ES2022 support and native ES modules (import()/type="module"): current Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari. The client runtime doesn't use any framework — it's plain JavaScript, so the real requirement is the JS engine, not a library.
compat.platformsBody: Web (any static host or reverse proxy) out of the box. nexa add tauri generates a real desktop binary for Windows/macOS/Linux. nexa add capacitor generates an Android/iOS project — the Android build was verified end to end (a real APK built with Gradle); iOS requires Xcode, which can't be built or verified on Linux.
compat.buildBody: The toolchain is written in Rust (the compiler) and TypeScript (the browser runtime). It was built and verified on Linux; Rust is cross-platform by design, so building on macOS should work the same way — that hasn't been verified yet in this round of phases. On Windows, the recommended path today is WSL.
compat.deployBody: dist/ is 100% static HTML/CSS/JS — any static host (Nginx, GitHub Pages, Cloudflare Pages, S3, whatever) serves it as is. nexa add nginx generates a real deploy/nginx.conf, with safe cache-busting for hashed files, if your host is a server you run yourself. This very site, in fact, is deployed on GitHub Pages — the same dist/, no nginx involved.

tutorialHub.title: Tutorial: from zero to production
tutorialHub.intro: Seventeen steps, each with real code. By the end you'll have a complete, deployed Nexa site.

install.title: Installation
install.intro: Nexa isn't published on crates.io or through an installer yet — you build it from source. You'll need Rust (for the compiler) and Node.js (for the TypeScript runtime packages).
install.s1Body: The compiler (crates/) and the browser runtime (packages/) live in the same repository.
install.s2Body: cargo build --release produces the nexa binary in target/release/. Add it to your PATH to use it from any project.
install.s3Body: nexa info should print the version and the toolchain's current phase.
install.s3Code:
nexa info
# Nexa CLI
# Version: 0.1.0
#
# Fase actual: 26 — ... (the CLI's own messages are Spanish-only today)

firstProject.title: Your first project
firstProject.intro: nexa create generates the minimal structure: one page, one manifest, and nothing else — no package.json, no node_modules.
firstProject.s1Body: This generates nexa.toml, nexa.config.ts and src/pages/index.tsx.
firstProject.s2Body: nexa build compiles src/pages/**/*.tsx into dist/ — real HTML, ready to serve.
firstProject.s3Body: cat dist/index.html — it's real HTML, with no JavaScript framework in the way.

routing.title: Routing
routing.intro: Routing is 100% file-based, over src/pages/. Every .tsx is a route; brackets mark dynamic segments.
routing.s1Body: pages/about.tsx is served at /about. pages/products/index.tsx is served at /products.
routing.s2Body: pages/products/[slug].tsx captures :slug and exposes it as params.slug — resolved on the fly with nexa preview/dev, or pre-rendered to static HTML if it declares paths (covered in the data step).
routing.s3Body: A route can combine several: pages/[locale]/products/[slug].tsx captures both at once — this very tutorial uses exactly that pattern for /es and /en.
routing.s3Code:
// src/pages/[locale]/products/[slug].tsx  ->  /:locale/products/:slug
// both params.locale and params.slug at once

data.title: Data with load()
data.intro: load is a plain object literal, not a function — Nexa Core never executes developer JavaScript, it only analyzes it. Declare a URL, and the result becomes available as data inside the page.
data.s1Body: :slug is substituted with the route's real parameter before requesting the URL against NEXA_API_URL.
data.s2Body: data.* is available in the JSX body, in seo, and in schema — resolved at build time or on the fly, depending on the command.
data.s3Body: If the page also declares paths (same shape as load), nexa build requests that list and generates a real index.html for each combination — genuinely static HTML, with no Nexa server running in production.
data.s4Body: A catalog, an article listing, a directory — <For> is one more syntactic pattern, recognized just like t() or onClick, never an arbitrary .map(): each only accepts data.x/params.x, and the callback returns a single JSX element per item. Before this, the only way to show a list was inside an island, losing the real HTML that is Nexa's whole reason to exist — with <For>, every <li> is indexable content from the very first byte.

seo.title: SEO and schema.org
seo.intro: seo and schema are static literals resolved against data/params — they generate real meta tags, Open Graph and JSON-LD, not a plugin that guesses.
seo.s1Body: title, description and canonical go straight into <head> — with data/params interpolation already resolved at build time.
seo.s2Body: schema generates a real <script type="application/ld+json">, valid for Google's Rich Results.
seo.s3Body: nexa build warns when a title, a description, or an image alt is missing — it never blocks the build, only warns. nexa lint can fail on purpose, for a CI step.
seo.s3Code: nexa build # [NEXA-SEO-001] missing `title` in `seo` # [NEXA-A11Y-001] with no `alt`

i18n.title: Internationalization
i18n.intro: A special [locale] route segment, plus t("key") in the body, seo and schema — resolved against src/locales/<locale>.json. This very tutorial you're reading uses exactly this mechanism.
i18n.s1Body: pages/[locale]/index.tsx is served at /es, /en, or any locale you have under src/locales/.
i18n.s2Body: t("key") recognizes one exact syntactic pattern: an identifier t with a single string literal — no dynamic key (t(variable) isn't recognized).
i18n.s3Body: When more than one locale is available, Nexa generates the <link rel="alternate" hreflang="..."> for every translation automatically.
i18n.s4Body: The second argument substitutes each variable placeholder in the text (see the example below) with a data.x/params.x reference — the same limited reference any other dynamic position in Nexa accepts, never a literal or an arbitrary expression. nexa build/nexa lint fail with a clear error if a key and its arguments don't match (a placeholder with no variable, or a leftover variable) — a broken, explicit build beats an unresolved placeholder shipped to production.
i18n.s3Code:
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="es" href="/es">
<link rel="alternate" hreflang="en" href="/en">

styling.title: Styling with @nexa/ui
styling.intro: Design tokens (with a real dark theme) + real CSS components (Button, Input, Card, Dialog, Drawer) + a small set of layout utilities, with real tree-shaking: the site only ships the CSS of what it actually uses. Deliberately small, not a full kit (see below for how to fill the gap fast if you need more).
styling.s1Body: No declaration needed — nexa build already detects nx-* classes and generates the matching CSS.
styling.s2Body: nexa add ui registers the module — it doesn't download anything (it's already embedded in the binary), it just makes nexa.toml reflect reality and stops nexa build from warning.
styling.s3Body: nexa-ui.css only carries the tokens plus the components the whole site actually uses — a fully static page in the same project doesn't link it at all.
styling.s4Title: How many components are there, and what if you need more?
styling.s4Body: Today there's Button, Input, Card, Dialog and Drawer (plus color/spacing/radius tokens and a small set of layout utilities, see below) — the full list, with every modifier, lives in docs/REFERENCIA.md in Nexa's repo. To put together a complete design fast you've got three paths, and all three use the same mechanism (a plain <link>, from the previous step): (1) write your own CSS from scratch — this very tutorial does exactly that, a hand-written site.css linked from the layout; (2) use Tailwind (via CDN to prototype, or your own build for production) plus a ready-made component kit built on Tailwind like DaisyUI or Flowbite; or (3) use Bootstrap, PrimeVue/PrimeReact, or whatever you prefer. @nexa/ui and a third-party framework aren't competing — you can use nx-btn for the simple stuff and Tailwind/Bootstrap for the rest of the layout, on the same page.
styling.s5Body: Not to be confused with platform.notify() (a real OS-level notification, from the native packaging step) — ui.notify() is an ephemeral notification inside the page, like Quasar's $q.notify(). It stacks with others, auto-closes after 4s (duration: 0 disables that), is accessible (role="status"), and needs no declaration: ui is already builtin, same as for Dialog.
styling.s6Body: Opening a second Dialog while the first is open really stacks now (correct z-index by depth, aria-hidden on whichever gets covered) — the focus trap was already isolated per dialog from the start. ui.confirm()/ui.alert() cover the common case of confirming before deleting something, or announcing something got saved, without hand-writing the <div class="nx-dialog">: they return a real Promise that resolves on Accept/Cancel/Escape. Drawer (for sidebars and menus) has the same trapped focus as Dialog, with its own CSS.
styling.s7Body: Without ever calling platform.theme.set(), the site already respects the OS's prefers-color-scheme — the helper (platform.theme.set("dark"|"light"|"system")) is only there so the user can pick explicitly and have that choice win over the system; it persists purely with platform.storage(), already covered. nx-flex/nx-grid/nx-stack are a small, deliberate set of layout utilities, tree-shaken just like the rest — not a full Tailwind-style utility system.
styling.s2Code:
nexa add ui
# Installed @nexa/ui v0.1.0 (stable).
# Registered in nexa.toml and nexa.lock.
styling.s3Code:
# dist/assets/nexa-ui.<hash>.css
# only ships tokens + .nx-btn — nothing from .nx-dialog if unused
styling.s4Code:
<!-- Tailwind Play CDN: fast for prototyping; compile the CSS for production -->
<script src="https://cdn.tailwindcss.com"></script>

<!-- ready-made components on top of Tailwind -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/daisyui@4/dist/full.min.css">

<!-- or, the classic choice -->
<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/bootstrap@5.3.3/dist/css/bootstrap.min.css">
styling.s7Code:
...
    ...

forms.title: Forms with @nexa/forms
forms.intro: Progressive enhancement over the browser's native Constraint Validation API — no proprietary rules, no reinventing HTML5 validation.
forms.s1Body: data-nexa-form activates the progressive enhancement; data-nexa-error-for shows the native validation message for the matching field.
forms.s2Body: initForms() is only injected if the page has a real <form data-nexa-form> — same criterion as the rest of Nexa.
forms.s2Code:
// No page without <form data-nexa-form> downloads @nexa/forms.
// Zero config, zero bytes when unused.

islands.title: Interactive islands
islands.intro: For what genuinely needs a real framework — a dashboard, a complex cart — without the rest of the site stopping being HTML-first.
islands.s1Body: The server only renders the fallback (the div's children, real content); mounting happens 100% on the client.
islands.s2Body: Any framework can implement this: hand-written code with @nexa/reactivity, or an adapter over Vue, Preact, whatever.
islands.s3Body: Rust never opens or interprets the specifier's module — to the compiler, a data-nexa-island is just another Element, like any other attribute.
islands.s4Title: The middle ground: a lightweight component model
islands.s4Body:
When an island needs more than a loose signal but doesn't justify loading a full external framework (a dropdown, a simple chat widget), @nexa/reactivity offers real composition — Component

typed by props, mountComponent() returning a cleanup function, and a ComponentContext (onCleanup/mount) that automatically chains a child's cleanup to its parent's. Still zero Virtual DOM, and exclusively for code inside a native island — never for Nexa Core pages. The same task-list widget that used to need full Vue 3 (~245KB) weighs ~4KB with this.

libraries.title: Third-party libraries and other frameworks
libraries.intro: Bootstrap, PrimeVue, a Chart.js graph, a Phaser game, or living alongside a whole Quasar, Vue, React or Angular app? Nexa doesn't replace any of that — it knows how to coexist with all of it, through a different mechanism depending on how "alive" the library is.
libraries.s1Body: Bootstrap, Tailwind via CDN, PrimeVue/PrimeReact's CSS — Nexa never processes or understands that CSS, so no special step is needed. A <link rel="stylesheet"> in src/layout.tsx (site-wide) or in a single page is enough.
libraries.s2Title: JS with a global (UMD) build: a plain <script>
libraries.s2Body: Bootstrap JS, Chart.js, and in general anything you can load as a classic <script> (not type="module") leaves a global variable (bootstrap, Chart, ...). Since a Nexa chunk copies the handler verbatim, you can use that global directly in an onClick — no need to declare anything in nexa.toml.
libraries.s3Title: Pure ES module libraries: the same [imports] as platform/stripe
libraries.s3Body: If the library is only distributed as an ES module (no global build), use [imports] — the same mechanism platform and stripe already use. The chunk detects <name>. in the handler and prepends the import; the import map in <head> resolves the specifier to the real URL.
libraries.s4Title: Full engines and frameworks: as an island
libraries.s4Body: For something with its own lifecycle — a Phaser game loop, or a stateful Vue/Quasar/React/Angular component tree — the answer is an island, not a loose [imports] in a handler. Your Quasar app compiles with ITS OWN build (Vite, same as always); Nexa never reads your .vue files or your React .tsx, it just serves the final bundle like any other JS. Important: even though Nexa's syntax looks like React (JSX, export default function), a Nexa page is NOT a React component — it compiles to static HTML once, with no VDOM, no hooks, no re-render. useState/useEffect don't work there; if you genuinely need that, it belongs inside an island using real React.
libraries.s2Code:
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/chart.js"></script>

function renderChart() {
    new Chart(document.getElementById("chart"), {
        type: "bar",
        data: { labels: ["Jan", "Feb"], datasets: [{ data: [10, 20] }] }
    });
}
libraries.s4Code:
Loading game…

// src/islands/game.island.ts — Phaser loaded as a global
libraries.s5Title: Vendoring a real npm package: the full guide
libraries.s5Body: When the package has its own dependencies or ships as CommonJS (the more common case, not just pure ESM from the point above), it needs a bundling step — install the package anywhere with npm, an entry.js re-exporting what's needed, and esbuild --bundle --format=esm into a single file, copied to public/vendor/. The full step-by-step process, with two real proven examples (with a wrapper, and without one), lives in docs/VENDORING.md in Nexa's repo.
libraries.s5Code:
mkdir vendor-build && cd vendor-build
npm install marked
echo 'export { marked } from "marked";' > entry.js
npx esbuild entry.js --bundle --format=esm --target=es2022 --outfile=marked.js
cp marked.js ../public/vendor/marked.js

# nexa.toml
[imports]
marked = "/vendor/marked.js"

realtime.title: Realtime: SSE and WebSocket
realtime.intro: connectSSE and connectSocket in @nexa/http wrap the browser's native APIs in reactive signals — no proprietary protocol.
realtime.s1Body: data is the last message received, parsed as JSON when possible.
realtime.s2Body: status reflects the connection's real lifecycle; send() automatically serializes objects as JSON.
realtime.s3Body: If the connection drops, reconnect: true (or a { maxAttempts, baseDelayMs, maxDelayMs } object to tune it) makes it reconnect on its own with exponential backoff + jitter — status goes through "reconnecting" while it tries. Verified by killing and restarting a real WebSocket server while a real browser kept the connection open. Without that option, it stays the same as always: status goes to "closed" and stays there.

layouts.title: Shared layouts
layouts.intro: An optional src/layout.tsx wraps every page's HTML — header, footer, nav — without reopening component composition.
layouts.s1Body: It must be empty, and there must be exactly one in the whole layout — that's where each page's already-rendered HTML gets inserted, verbatim.
layouts.s2Body: The layout compiles just like any page. Neither the layout nor the page know about each other before that final splice.
layouts.s3Title: export const head: the one thing that really reaches <head>
layouts.s3Body: Everything else the layout returns ends up inside <body> (via the splice above) — a <link rel="icon"> placed there gets stuck in <body>, where not every browser detects it reliably (this very site had exactly that bug). export const head = { icon, appleTouchIcon, stylesheets } is resolved separately and merged into the document's real <head> — same pattern as seo/schema, a literal object, never executed code.
layouts.s4Title: Islands in the layout, and navigation without reloading the header
layouts.s4Body: An event of the layout's own still makes the build fail (its ids would share a manifest with each page's) — but an island CAN live there, and it survives SPA navigation intact: a user dropdown with real state, for example. Also, once a project uses a layout, navigating between pages no longer replaces the whole <body>: only the content inside data-nexa-slot changes, so the layout's header/nav (and its island, if it has one) never gets torn down between one page and the next.
layouts.s4Code:
// src/layout.tsx — the island lives outside data-nexa-slot, // survives every navigation

Loading…

pwa.title: Declarative PWA
pwa.intro: nexa add pwa adds a real [pwa] block to nexa.toml — nexa build generates a real manifest.webmanifest and a real service worker, not an empty template.
pwa.s1Body: name, icon, colors and display mode — all real, without hand-writing a manifest.json.
pwa.s2Body: cache-first, network-first, or stale-while-revalidate per route prefix, declared under [pwa.cache].

images.title: Optimized images
images.intro: nexa build optimizes any static on its own, with no developer effort: real AVIF variants, HTML rewritten to .
images.s1Body: Any static image under public/ is detected and optimized automatically during the build.
images.s2Body: The browser only downloads the smallest AVIF it needs for its viewport — never the fallback original, unless the browser doesn't support AVIF.

performance.title: Performance budgets
performance.intro: nexa.toml can declare JS/CSS/image limits per page — unlike SEO warnings, this one genuinely blocks the build.
performance.s1Body: Absent by default (zero friction); declared, it's actually enforced.
performance.s2Body: The framework assets the bootstrap always loads, plus chunks with the load strategy — the ones deferred on purpose (interaction/visible/idle/manual) don't count.
performance.s2Code:
nexa build
# Presupuesto de rendimiento excedido (1 página(s)):
#   /products: maxInitialJS usa 18204 bytes, supera 15000
# Error: el build no cumple el presupuesto de nexa.toml

native.title: Native packaging and @nexa/platform
native.intro: The same source code compiles to a real desktop binary (Tauri), a real APK (Capacitor Android), or a real Xcode project (Capacitor iOS) — without rewriting anything. Web, desktop, Android and iOS from a single project, and @nexa/platform is what makes the same handler work across all three with no branches of your own.
native.s1Body: Generates a real src-tauri/ — cargo build produces a real, runnable desktop binary on Windows, macOS and Linux.
native.s2Body: Requires the Android SDK installed — the result is a real APK, built with Gradle. Verified end to end with a real SDK.
native.s3Body: Same capacitor.config.json as Android — add ios generates a real Xcode project (ios/). Needs macOS with Xcode to build: not tested in this Linux environment, but the mechanism is identical to Android's.
native.s4Body: platform.share()/platform.notify()/platform.capturePhoto() call the real Capacitor plugin on Android/iOS (@capacitor/share, etc.) and the standard Web API on web and inside Tauri's webview — without the project writing any branch of its own. platform.storage()/platform.sessionStorage() wrap localStorage/sessionStorage with the same contract across all three environments; platform.cache() gives direct access to the Cache API (no [pwa] declaration needed); platform.db("name") is a minimal wrapper over IndexedDB, with nothing to declare upfront. Every function throws a clear Error if the capability isn't available — never fails silently.
native.s5Body: platform.theme.set("dark"|"light"|"system") persists the preference and lets it win over the system's prefers-color-scheme (never calling it, the site already respects that). platform.network.getStatus()/onChange() give the real connectivity state (online/offline, plus the connection type on Capacitor); platform.lifecycle.getState()/onChange() report when the app goes to the background or comes back — via @capacitor/app on Capacitor, via document.hidden/visibilitychange on web. It grows one module at a time, based on real need: geolocation, deep links, real push, biometrics and haptics aren't there yet.
native.s1Code:
nexa add tauri
cd src-tauri && cargo build
# a real, runnable desktop binary
native.s2Code:
nexa add capacitor
npx @capacitor/cli add android
cd android && ./gradlew assembleDebug
# real APK at app/build/outputs/apk/debug/
native.s3Code:
nexa add capacitor
npx @capacitor/cli add ios
npx cap open ios
# opens the real project in Xcode (requires macOS)

production.title: Going to production
production.intro: The final stretch: lint, test, and a real deploy — the same path this very site followed, published on GitHub Pages.
production.s1Body: Compiles every page without writing dist/ and fails if the SEO Analyzer or package warnings found anything — meant to block a merge in CI.
production.s2Body: Compiles the project (a fresh dist/, with the Fase 23 hashed filenames) and runs the project's JS test runner against that build.
production.s3Body: Generates a real deploy/nginx.conf: gzip, security headers, and a year-long immutable cache only for the files that genuinely carry a content hash.
production.s4Title: Dynamic routes with no paths, in real production
production.s4Body: A route that doesn't declare paths (its parameter space can't be enumerated upfront) still can't be pre-rendered — but nexa add nginx also generates a real proxy_pass towards a nexa preview running behind it, tested end to end against a real backend: not "run the dev server in prod", a documented and verified mechanism.
production.s5Body: dist/ is 100% static — any host serves it. This complete tutorial ends here: you now have what it takes to take a real Nexa project to production.
production.s1Code:
nexa lint
# [NEXA-SEO-001] missing `title` in `seo`
# Error: `nexa lint` found warnings
production.s2Code:
nexa test
# Compiling the project before running tests...
# Running `npm test`...
production.s3Code:
nexa add nginx
# Generates deploy/nginx.conf — gzip, security headers,
# a year-long immutable cache only for hashed files.
